                     Electronic Colloquium on Computational Complexity, Report No. 229 (2026)




           A POLYNOMIAL SCALING WINDOW FOR RANDOM k-SAT
            AND A PROOF OF THE SATISFIABILITY CONJECTURE

                                                 GAIA CARENINI


        Abstract. We prove that the scaling window of random k-SAT has width O(n1/2+1/k ), a polyno-
        mial improvement over our previous bound of O(n/ log n). Combined with a result of Abbe and
        Montanari, this establishes the satisfiability conjecture for every fixed k ≥ 3: there exists a constant
        αk such that a random k-SAT formula on n variables with ⌊αn⌋ clauses is satisfiable with high
        probability if α < αk and unsatisfiable with high probability if α > αk .




                                                1. Introduction
   How many random clauses are needed to make a Boolean formula unsatisfiable? For random
k-SAT, a sharp transition is known to occur, but sharpness and convergence of the transition density
are different questions. The purpose of this paper is to obtain a sufficiently strong quantitative
form of sharpness to settle the latter question as well.
   Let Cn be the(︁ set of signed k-clauses on [n] = {1, . . . , n}, each with k distinct variables, and let
                k n)︁
Nn = |Cn | = 2 k . This is the Boolean case of the notation in [7], with the fixed alphabet size and
clause length suppressed. Let Fn,m be the conjunction of m independent uniform members of Cn ;
repetitions between clauses are allowed. The parameter α = m/n is the clause density. Throughout
the paper, k is fixed and n → ∞, and an event holds with high probability if its probability tends to
one.
   Early experiments revealed a pronounced transition in the satisfiability of random formulas as
the clause density increases. Mitchell, Selman and Levesque [12] observed that the computational
effort of the satisfiability procedure they tested peaked near this transition. These observations
helped motivate two closely related lines of research: determining when a random formula has a
solution, and understanding the difficulty of finding or certifying the absence of one.
   The satisfiability conjecture asserts that, for every fixed k ≥ 3, there is a constant αk such that
Fn,⌊αn⌋ is satisfiable with high probability for α < αk and unsatisfiable with high probability for
α > αk . Thus the transition is conjectured to occur at a limiting clause density independent of n.
In this paper, we prove the conjecture.
   A major advance towards the conjecture was Friedgut’s sharp-threshold theorem [10], with an
appendix by Bourgain. For every fixed k ≥ 3, it gives a sequence αk (n), bounded above and
bounded away from zero, such that, for every fixed η > 0, formulas of density αk (n) − η are
satisfiable with high probability, whereas formulas of density αk (n) + η are unsatisfiable with high
probability. The remaining issue is convergence of αk (n). Sharpness alone does not exclude the
possibility that the location of the transition varies with n without approaching a limit.
   For 2-SAT, the limiting threshold is α2 = 1, and Bollobás, Borgs, Chayes, Kim and Wilson [6]
determined the scaling window to have width Θ(n2/3 ) clauses. For larger k, first- and second-
moment arguments gave increasingly precise bounds on the critical density [2, 3, 4]. In particular,
Achlioptas and Peres [4] located the transition within an additive O(k) of 2k log 2. Such estimates
describe the threshold as k grows, while leaving open its convergence as n → ∞ for each fixed k.
   Ding, Sly and Sun [8] proved the satisfiability conjecture for all sufficiently large k. They also
identified the limiting threshold with the value predicted by the one-step replica symmetry breaking
cavity method from statistical physics. Their proof develops a detailed analysis of the organisation
of solutions into clusters, combining moment calculations with conditioning on local neighbourhood
statistics and the analysis of recursions on trees. These methods establish both the existence and
                                                           1




                                                                                                                   ISSN 1433-8092

the value of the threshold, but involve substantial probabilistic and analytic machinery whose
extension to every fixed k ≥ 3 presents significant difficulties.
    A different route is suggested by Abbe and Montanari [1], who connect the width of the transition
to convergence of its location. We retain the window notation of [7]. Let Covern ⊆ 2Cn be the event
of unsatisfiability, and let µp include each clause independently with probability p. For u ∈ (0, 1),
set pu (n) = inf{p : µp (Covern ) ≥ u}. For η ∈ (0, 1/2), the independent-inclusion window, measured
in expected clause count, is Wη (n) = Nn (p1−η (n) − pη (n)). For sampling with replacement, let
m˜︁ u (n) be the least m for which P(Fn,m is unsatisfiable) ≥ u, and set W          m1−η (n) − m
                                                                          ˜︂η (n) = ˜︁         ˜︁ η (n).

satisfiability conjecture follows if, for some fixed δ > 0 and every fixed η ∈ (0, 1/2),

The criterion is stated for the independent-inclusion model; Section 4 gives the transfer between
the two models. Thus a sufficiently strong quantitative improvement in sharpness establishes a
limiting threshold density.

of a general theorem for sparse monotone covering problems. That argument combines the
strengthening of Bourgain’s theorem by Keevash, Lifshitz, Long and Minzer [11] with a comparison
between the effects of prescribed local constraints and additional random constraints. It also gives
windows of the same order for random signed NAE-k-SAT and hypergraph non-two-colourability.

k-SAT to a polynomial scale.

Theorem 1.1 with the Abbe–Montanari criterion yields the following consequence.
Corollary 1.2 (Satisfiability conjecture). For every fixed k ≥ 3, there exists αk ∈ (0, ∞) such that,

   To prove the window estimate, we couple all clause counts on one probability space. Choose an
infinite sequence C1 , C2 , . . . of independent uniform signed k-clauses and let Fn,m = C1 ∧ · · · ∧ Cm ,
with Fn,0 the empty formula. Clauses are added one at a time, and once the formula becomes
unsatisfiable it remains so. Let Tn be the first unsatisfiable clause count and put an = ETn . Since
P(Fn,m is unsatisfiable) = P(Tn ≤ m), the window is a quantile interval for Tn . We prove the
following stronger statement.
Theorem 1.3. For every fixed k ≥ 3, there exists Ck < ∞ such that Var(Tn ) ≤ Ck n1+2/k .
Consequently, for every x > 0,

                                                              x2
  Theorem 1.1 follows immediately by Chebyshev’s inequality. The variance estimate also controls
probabilities tending to zero, beyond the fixed probability levels used to define the scaling window.
  Wilson [14, Corollary 4] proved the lower bound W˜︂η (n) = Ωk,η (n1/2 ), including in the fixed-clause
model. Our upper bound leaves a gap of 1/k between the exponents. Section 5 discusses this gap
and the two estimates from which our exponent arises.

1.1. Motivation and the change of approach. The starting point is the local comparison
in our earlier work [7], rather than the sharp-threshold theorem in which it was used. In that
argument, a wide transition leads, through the quantitative Bourgain theorem of Keevash, Lifshitz,
Long and Minzer [11], to a small prescribed collection of constraints whose addition increases
the probability of unsatisfiability. The replacement step reproduces part of this increase using
genuinely random constraints. At a scale K ≍ n/Wη (n), the guaranteed increase is exponentially
small in K, and its simulation uses at most exponentially many   √ random constraints. The general
                                                              ′
random-coordinate increment bound then gives e−CK ≲ eC K / n. This forces K = Ω(log n), and
hence gives O(n/ log n) for the window. Changing constants or repeating the same comparison
does not give another power of the logarithm. This is a limitation of that quantitative argument,
not a barrier to every possible use of Friedgut–Bourgain theory.
   The replacement principle contains more information than this application uses. Its underlying
comparison between shorter clauses and k-clauses holds for every residual set of assignments; no
booster is needed to state it. Moreover, shorter clauses arise whenever we fix a variable. This
suggests applying the comparison to the two possible values of a single variable, and doing so
throughout the clause process rather than only at a density selected by a sharp-threshold theorem.
   The natural probabilistic framework for this change of approach is that of structured coupon
collectors. Each clause covers the assignments that falsify it, so unsatisfiability occurs precisely
when these random codimension-k subcubes cover {0, 1}n . This interpretation is discussed explicitly
by Falgas-Ravry, Larsson and Markström [9, Section 5.4]. The same paper recalls Aldous’s
concentration criterion [9, Section 2.2, Theorem 2]: a cover time is concentrated when the expected
time to cover its last uncovered set using a fresh independent continuation is small compared with
the expected cover time. In the clause process, this last uncovered set is exactly the solution set of
the last satisfiable formula. Aldous’s quantitative inequality [5, Theorem 1(b)] therefore suggests
estimating the remaining lifetime of this formula, rather than seeking a local witness through a
sharp-threshold theorem.
   Two choices make this useful. Forced variables describe exactly how a single clause can eliminate
the remaining solutions. The expected remaining time describes how resistant those solutions are
to a fresh sequence of clauses, and has a simple conditional drift. Aldous’s covering inequality
connects the latter quantity to the variance of Tn . The argument below explains how deleting one
variable connects the two quantities to each other.

1.2. Overview of the proof. We shall not try to describe the whole set of satisfying assignments.
Instead, we ask how long that set would survive if we continued adding independent random clauses.
The proof turns this remaining lifetime into an estimate for the fluctuations of Tn .

Why look at the last satisfiable formula? For a satisfiable formula G on n variables, let rn (G) be
the expected number of further independent uniform k-clauses needed to make it unsatisfiable; set
rn (G) = 0 if it is already unsatisfiable. The elementary first-moment bound gives rn (G) ≤ an =
Ok (n). Let Γn = Fn,Tn −1 . Although the next clause in the observed process destroys Γn , this does
not show that rn (Γn ) is small: the observed clause has been selected by the fact that it succeeded,
whereas rn is defined using a fresh independent continuation.
   Each clause excludes a codimension-k subcube of {0, 1}n , and unsatisfiability means that these
subcubes cover the whole cube. Aldous’s inequality [5, Theorem 1(b)] gives Var(Tn ) ≤ κan Ern (Γn ).
Thus it is enough to prove
                                         Ern (Γn ) = Ok (n2/k ).                                (1.2)
The question about the whole process has become a question about the difficulty of eliminating its
last surviving solutions.

What does the final clause tell us? Suppose, for example, that adjoining x1 ∨ ¬x2 ∨ x3 makes a
satisfiable formula unsatisfiable. Every original solution must have x1 = 0, x2 = 1 and x3 = 0.
Thus every variable in a clause that ends the process was already forced. Here a variable is forced
4                                            G. CARENINI

if it has the same value in every satisfying assignment, not merely in the assignments belonging to
one cluster.
    As in the cubical notation of [7], write ℓ(G) for the number of coordinates fixed throughout
the solution set, and ρj (G) for the probability that one uniform signed j-clause destroys G. We
apply these symbols directly to a formula rather than naming its solution set separately. Then
ρj (G) = ℓ(G)     j n
          (︁   )︁  (︁ )︁
             j /(2 j ). The clause must choose only forced coordinates and then choose the unique
sign pattern disagreeing with their forced values. The solution set may be complicated, but its
probability of being destroyed by one clause is determined by a single integer.
    We can now identify the estimate we need. Besides rn (G) ≤ an , we have rn (G) ≤ 1/ρk (G)
whenever ρk (G) > 0: simply wait for a clause that eliminates every original solution, ignoring any
help from intervening clauses. Consequently,
                                                                  1/k

                           ρk (G)rn (G) ≤ min{1, an ρk (G)} ≤              .

A satisfiable state is selected as the last one with conditional probability ρk (G). Summing over the
possible times of the final transition therefore shows that (1.2) follows from
                                                  ℓ(Fn,m )

                                                     n
This is an integrated estimate: it bounds the expected total time for which a uniformly chosen
variable is forced before unsatisfiability. We do not need to show that every formula encountered
by the process has few forced variables.

How can we recognise a forced variable? Fix a variable x and delete all clauses containing it, leaving
a formula G on the other n − 1 variables. Each choice x = 0 or x = 1 restores some of the deleted
clauses as (k − 1)-clauses, while satisfying the others automatically. Exactly one branch survives
when the original formula is satisfiable and forces x.
   Let clauses arrive according to a rate-one Poisson process. At time t, the clauses avoiding x,
those containing x, and those containing ¬x form independent families. Conditional on G, the two
branches are therefore independent and identically distributed. Each adjoins a Poisson number
of shorter clauses of mean z = kt/(2n). If qG (z) is its probability of failure, then the conditional
probability that the full formula is satisfiable and forces x is 2qG (z)(1 − qG (z)) for satisfiable
G. Deletion turns a statement about all solutions into a comparison between two independent
perturbations of a common formula.
   For t = Ok (n) the mean z is bounded. The replacement lemma gives qG (z) ≤ Ck,L rn−1 (G)−(k−1)/k
for 0 ≤ z ≤ L. The power comes from the exact formula for ρj : up to finite-size corrections, ρk is
the k/(k − 1)-th power of ρk−1 . Several shorter clauses may nevertheless cooperate, so a one-step
comparison at the initial formula is not enough. We add both clause lengths, apply the comparison
at every intermediate state, and integrate while replacing shorter clauses by ordinary ones. If
r = rn−1 (G), an independent-block argument bounds the probability of failure after time t by t/r.
The interpolation costs Ok,L (t−(k−1) ), apart from a finite-size error. Taking t = r1/k balances these
two terms and gives the stated power of r.

Why does the contribution not accumulate too much? The advantage of rn is the exact first-step
identity E[rn (H ∧ C)] = rn (H) − 1 for satisfiable H. If rn decreased deterministically by one at each
                 −(k−1)/k                        1/k
step, summing rn ∫︁       would cost only Ok (an ). It need not behave in this way, but the concave
                    r
potential Φ(r) = 0 (1 + u)−(k−1)/k du gives the same bound in expectation. Each contribution
is bounded by a constant multiple of the expected decrease of Φ; the decreases telescope. No
concentration of rn itself is required.
   The deleted formula has the law of the same clause process on n − 1 variables, with time
rescaled by 1 − k/n. We may therefore apply this occupation estimate to it. The deletion identity
and replacement lemma give (1.3) up to any sufficiently large constant multiple of n, and the
                        A POLYNOMIAL SCALING WINDOW FOR RANDOM k-SAT                                   5

first-moment bound controls the remaining tail. Poisson time preserves the discrete occupation
sums exactly.
   There are now two factors of n1/k : one from total forcing and one from the conversion to
the terminal distribution. They give Ern (Γn ) = Ok (n2/k ), and Aldous’s inequality yields the
variance bound. Chebyshev gives the window. Convergence of the threshold density is a separate
final step, obtained from the Abbe–Montanari criterion after transferring the estimate to the
independent-inclusion model.
   Section 2 proves the replacement lemma; Section 3 gives the occupation and deletion estimates;
and Section 4 completes the variance bound and the passage to a limiting density. Section 5
considers the remaining gap to the lower bound.

             2. Remaining expected time and replacement of shorter clauses
   Fix k ≥ 3. All logarithms are natural, and constants may depend on k. We use the clause family
Cn , the process Fn,m , and the mean an = ETn defined above. For an arbitrary satisfiable formula
G on [n], define
                    rn (G) = E min{m ≥ 1 : G ∧ C1 ∧ · · · ∧ Cm is unsatisfiable},
where the clauses are independent of G, and set rn (G) = 0 if G is unsatisfiable. The formula G
need not be a k-CNF; this allows the same definition after adding shorter clauses.
  Expose the clauses at the arrival times of an independent rate-one Poisson process (Πt )t≥0 , and
write Fn (t) = Fn,Πt . Let τn be its first unsatisfiable time and sn (t) = P(τn > t). Conditional on Tn ,
the variable τn is a sum of Tn independent exponential random variables of mean one. Consequently,
                               Eτn = an ,      Var(τn ) = Var(Tn ) + an .                          (2.1)
Every fixed assignment satisfies a uniform signed k-clause with probability 1 − 2−k . A union bound
over assignments therefore gives

  We next express the effect of shorter clauses in terms of the remaining expected time. This is
the form of replacement used in the rest of the proof.
Lemma 2.1. Fix L < ∞. For a satisfiable formula G on n ≥ k variables, let qG (z) be the probability

Remark 2.2. The shorter clauses can create new forced variables and thereby make later clauses
more effective. For example, the four signed 2-clauses on two variables are jointly inconsistent,
although none alone destroys the empty formula. A union bound based only on the initial value of
ρk−1 (G) therefore cannot replace the interpolation. The differential inequality (2.8) is applied to
the evolving formula, which is why it accounts for cooperation between the shorter clauses.

                     3. Occupation estimates and deletion of a variable
   The remaining expected time need not decrease by a comparable amount on every step. Its
conditional expected decrease is nevertheless exactly one. A concave potential converts this identity
into a bound on the sum of inverse powers along the process. An expression multiplied by the
indicator of satisfiability is defined to be zero at an unsatisfiable formula, including when it contains
a negative power of rn .
Lemma 3.1. For every λ > 0,

  Passing to Poisson time preserves these occupation sums exactly. For every nonnegative function
f of the formula, independence of Πt and the clauses gives

   Write βn (t) = E[1{Fn (t) is satisfiable} ℓ(Fn (t))/n] for the expected proportion of forced variables,
counted only before unsatisfiability. We estimate its integral by deleting one variable. Assume
n > k, fix a variable x, and partition the clauses present at time t into those avoiding x, those
containing x, and those containing ¬x. Poisson splitting makes these three families independent.
The formula G formed by the first family has the law of Fn−1 ((1 − k/n)t). Each of the other
two families has a Poisson number of clauses with mean z = kt/(2n). After removing the literal
involving x, its clauses are independent uniform signed (k − 1)-clauses on the other variables.
Setting x = 0 retains the shortened positive family and satisfies the negative family automatically;
setting x = 1 does the reverse. Conditional on a satisfiable G, the two resulting formulas are
therefore independent, and each is unsatisfiable with probability qG (z).
   Exactly one branch being satisfiable is equivalent to the full formula being satisfiable and forcing
x. Both branches being unsatisfiable is equivalent to the full formula being unsatisfiable. By
exchangeability of the variables,
                                                     [︂                                         ]︂
                                  βn (t) = 2E 1{G is satisfiable} qG (z)(1 − qG (z)) ,                  (3.3)
                                                [︂                                        ]︂
                                  sn (t) = E 1{G is satisfiable} (1 − qG (z)2 ) .                       (3.4)
These identities use only the Poisson splitting and the two possible values of a Boolean variable.

                   4. Variance, scaling windows, and the limiting density
   We now use the occupation estimate to bound the remaining expected time at the last satisfiable
formula. The link to the variance is the following general covering theorem.
Theorem 4.1 (Aldous [5], Theorem 1(b)). Let X be a nonempty finite set, and let Y1 , Y2 , . . . be
independent copies of a random subset of X such   that P(x ∈ Y1 ) > 0 for every x ∈ X. Let T be the
first time these sets cover X, and let T = X \ i<T Yi be the last uncovered set. For deterministic
                                               ⋃︁

A ⊆ X, let c(A) be the expected time to cover A using a fresh independent sequence with the same
law. There is an absolute constant κ such that
                                                  Var(T ) ≤ κ ET E[c(T )].
Proof of Theorem 1.3. Take X = {0, 1}n and let Yi be the assignments falsifying Ci . Each assign-
ment belongs to Yi with probability 2−k , and the resulting cover time is Tn . If Γn = Fn,Tn −1 , then
the terminal uncovered set is the solution set of Γn . Thus Theorem 4.1 gives
                                                  Var(Tn ) ≤ κan Ern (Γn ).                                        (4.1)
   For any satisfiable G with ρk (G) > 0, waiting for a clause that by itself excludes every original
solution of G shows that rn (G) ≤ 1/ρk (G). Together with rn (G) ≤ an , this yields
                                                                                              1/k

                      ρk (G)rn (G) ≤ min{1, an ρk (G)} ≤ a1/k
                                                          n ρk (G)

The last inequality follows from ℓ(G)    n               k
                                        (︁        )︁ (︁ )︁
                                    k / k ≤ (ℓ(G)/n) when ℓ(G) ≥ k; if ℓ(G) < k, the left-hand
side is zero. The estimate therefore holds in all cases.
   Decompose according to the final transition. Since {Tn = m + 1} occurs when Fn,m is satisfiable
and the next clause makes it unsatisfiable, conditioning on the first m clauses gives
                                                  ∑︂         [︂                     ]︂

Using an = Ok (n) in (4.1) proves Var(Tn ) = Ok (n1+2/k ). The stated tail estimate follows from
Chebyshev’s inequality.                                                                        □
Proof of Theorem 1.1. The identity P(F√︁  n,m is unsatisfiable) = P(Tn ≤ m) identifies m
                                                                                       ˜︁ u (n) with the
corresponding quantile of Tn . Set d = 2 Var(Tn )/η. Chebyshev’s inequality gives P(|Tn − an | ≥
d) ≤ η/2, so both quantiles defining W˜︂η (n) lie between an − d and an + d, up to integer rounding.
Thus W˜︂η (n) ≤ 2d + 2 = Ok,η (n1/2+1/k ).                                                            □

  To apply the criterion for a limiting density, we transfer the estimate to µp on 2Cn . Recall
that Wη (n) = Nn (p1−η (n) − pη (n)). As in [7], let W
                                                     ˆ︂η (n) denote the corresponding window for a
uniformly chosen set of distinct clauses.
Proposition 4.2. For every fixed k ≥ 3 and η ∈ (0, 1/2),
                                       Wη (n) = Ok,η (n1/2+1/k ).                                  (4.3)
The same bound holds for W
                         ˆ︂η (n).

Proof. By (2.1) and Theorem 1.3, Var(τn ) = Ok (n1+2/k ). Its fixed-level quantile window is therefore
Ok,η (n1/2+1/k ). Poisson splitting shows that at time t the multiplicities of the Nn possible clauses
are independent Poisson variables of mean t/Nn . Since repetitions do not affect satisfiability,
P(Fn (t) is unsatisfiable) = µp(t) (Covern ) for p(t) = 1 − e−t/Nn . As Nn p′ (t) = e−t/Nn ≤ 1, the
change of parameter does not increase the quantile window when it is measured in expected clause
count. This proves (4.3).
   For the model without replacement, fix a sufficiently large constant K = K(k). Among the first
⌈Kn⌉ independent draws, the probability of a repeated clause is at most ⌈Kn⌉         /Nn = Ok (n2−k ) =
                                                                             (︁   )︁
                                                                                2
o(1). Conditioned on no repetitions, the ordered sequence is uniform among sequences of distinct
clauses. Thus the satisfiability probabilities in the two models differ by o(1) uniformly for m ≤ Kn.
The discrete bound in (2.2) places all fixed central quantiles below Kn. For large n, the without-
replacement window from η to 1 − η is contained between the with-replacement quantiles at levels
η/2 and 1 − η/2. Theorem 1.1 now gives the assertion.                                                 □
   We use the Abbe–Montanari criterion [1] in the form stated in [13, Proposition 14]: if, for some
fixed δ > 0 and every fixed η ∈ (0, 1/2), the independent-inclusion window satisfies Wη (n) =
Ok,η (Nn p1/2 (n)/(log n)1+δ ), then the satisfiability threshold has a limiting clause density. The
standard linear bounds on the critical number of clauses give Nn p1/2 (n) = Θk (n); see, for example, [7,
Corollary 7.6] with alphabet size two. Thus the criterion has exactly the expected-clause-count
normalization used in (1.1).

Proof of Corollary 1.2. Since 1/2 + 1/k < 1, Proposition 4.2 gives Wη (n) = Ok,η (n1/2+1/k ) =
o(n/(log n)2 ). The Abbe–Montanari criterion, with δ = 1, therefore yields a limiting density
αk ∈ (0, ∞) in the independent-inclusion model.
   For clarity, we give the transfer back to a fixed number of independent clauses. At time
t = αn, the corresponding independent-inclusion model has expected clause count Nn p(αn) =
αn + Ok (n2 /Nn ) = αn + o(1). Monotonicity therefore gives sn (αn) → 1 for fixed α < αk , and
sn (αn) → 0 for fixed α > αk . If 0 ≤ α < αk , choose α′ ∈ (α, αk ) and couple Fn,⌊αn⌋ and Fn (α′ n)
using the same clause sequence. Then
         P(Fn,⌊αn⌋ is unsatisfiable) ≤ P(Fn (α′ n) is unsatisfiable) + P(Πα′ n < ⌊αn⌋) −→ 0.
If α > αk , choose α′ ∈ (αk , α) and similarly obtain
                    P(Fn,⌊αn⌋ is satisfiable) ≤ sn (α′ n) + P(Πα′ n > ⌊αn⌋) −→ 0.
The Poisson error probabilities vanish because their means and the comparison counts differ by
order n. This proves the corollary.                                                         □
10                                            G. CARENINI

  The mean hitting time converges to the same limiting density, and the variance estimate gives a
polynomial error probability at any fixed positive distance from it.
Corollary 4.3. We have an /n → αk . Moreover, for every fixed d ∈ (0, αk ),
                       P(Fn,⌊(αk −d)n⌋ is unsatisfiable)
                             + P(Fn,⌈(αk +d)n⌉ is satisfiable) = Ok,d (n−1+2/k ).
Proof. Corollary 1.2 gives Tn /n → αk in probability. Theorem 1.3 gives (Tn − an )/n → 0 in
probability, so the deterministic sequence an /n also converges to αk . For all sufficiently large n,
|an /n − αk | < d/2. Each event in the displayed estimate then implies a deviation of Tn from an by
at least dn/2. Applying Theorem 1.3 completes the proof.                                           □

                                   5. Remarks and questions
5.1. The lower bound and the possible window exponent. Wilson [14, Corollary 4] proved
˜︂η (n) = Ωk,η (n1/2 ) for every fixed k and η ∈ (0, 1/2). This holds when the number of clauses is
W
fixed, both with and without replacement. It is therefore not merely a consequence of fluctuations
in the clause count of a Poisson or independent-inclusion model. The proof uses clauses containing
a variable that occurs nowhere else in the formula: such clauses can be removed without changing
satisfiability.
   Together with Theorem 1.1, this gives
                                  ck,η n1/2 ≤ W
                                              ˜︂η (n) ≤ Ck,η n1/2+1/k .

For 3-SAT, the bounds are Ωη (n1/2 ) and Oη (n5/6 ). The present proof does not establish that the
upper exponent is sharp. It records the cost of two estimates, neither of which is shown to be
attained along the random process.
                                                         ˜︂η (n) = Ok,η (n1/2 )? More modestly, is
Question 5.1. For every fixed k ≥ 3 and η ∈ (0, 1/2), is W
˜︂η (n) = n1/2+o(1) ?
W
   The lower bound alone gives no reason that equality should hold. In particular, the 2-SAT
window has the larger order Θ(n2/3 ) [6]. A square-root upper bound for k ≥ 3 would need additional
information about the process, not just its monotonicity.
5.2. Where the two factors ∫︁of n1/k enter. Two bounds contribute to the terminal expectation.
The occupation estimate gives 0∞ βn (t) dt = Ok (n1/k ), and the passage to terminal sampling gives
                                                  1/k ∫︂ ∞
                                                  an
                                    Ern (Γn ) ≤              βn (t) dt.
                                                   2   0
Thus Ern (Γn ) = Ok (n2/k ) has two separate sources.
   The first is the occupation bound.      Replacement gives the inverse power r−(k−1)/k , and the
                                     ∫︁ an−1
potential argument sums it at a cost 0       (1 + u)−(k−1)/k du = Ok (n1/k ). The bound uses the initial
remaining lifetime and its conditional drift, but not a more detailed description of the states visited
by the process. A smaller accumulated contribution could therefore hold for random formulas even
if the replacement estimate is optimal for arbitrary residual solution sets.
   The second factor arises in passing to the terminal distribution. We use only
                                                                           1/k
                                                                       an ℓ(G)
                   ρk (G)rn (G) ≤ min{1, an ρk (G)} ≤ a1/k
                                                       n ρk (G)
                                                                1/k
                                                                    ≤          .
                                                                        2   n
The scalar inequality min{1, x} ≤ x1/k is sharp at x = 1. This does not show that states near
equality carry a substantial part of the occupation measure. In particular, the estimate discards
information about the joint behaviour of ρk (G) and rn (G), and about the further forcing created
by subsequent clauses. The upper bound on Ern (Γn ) should not be read as a determination of a
typical terminal lifetime, or as a count of the last surviving assignments.
                         A POLYNOMIAL SCALING WINDOW FOR RANDOM k-SAT                                  11

   There is also a limit to sharpening the pointwise comparison alone. Consider a subcube with b
fixed coordinates, where b → ∞ and b/n → 0. For its solution set, equation (2.5) gives ρj ≍k (b/n)j
for j ∈ {k − 1, k}. Thus the power k/(k − 1) in the comparison of ρk with ρk−1 cannot be decreased
uniformly over arbitrary residual solution sets. This does not establish sharpness of the replacement
lemma or of the window bound. It suggests looking for information about which states the clause
process visits, or how it moves between them, rather than only improving the one-step comparison.
5.3. A question about the last surviving solutions. The covering inequality provides a
concrete sufficient target for a square-root window.
Question 5.2. For each fixed k ≥ 3, is supn≥k Ern (Γn ) < ∞? More modestly, does Ern (Γn ) = no(1)
hold?
   A bounded terminal expectation would give Var(Tn ) = Ok (n), and hence an upper bound
matching Wilson’s lower bound. A subpolynomial terminal expectation would give W            ˜︂η (n) =
n 1/2+o(1) . These are sufficient conditions; the corresponding fixed-level window estimates need not
by themselves control all the tails required for a variance bound.
   The distinction between an expectation and a high-probability statement is important here. For
example, suppose that ℓ(Γn ) ≥ cn outside an event of probability δn , for some fixed c > 0. On
that event’s complement, the one-clause destruction probability is bounded away from zero, so
rn (Γn ) = Ok,c (1). On the exceptional event we have only rn (Γn ) = Ok (n). These two bounds give
Ern (Γn ) = Ok,c (1) + Ok (nδn ). Thus a qualitative high-probability assertion would not alone prove
a bounded terminal expectation. No such assertion about ℓ(Γn ) is needed in the present argument.
   The exact terminal identity is
                                          ∑︂      [︂                          ]︂
                            Ern (Γn ) =         E 1{Tn >m} ρk (Fn,m )rn (Fn,m ) .
                                          m≥0
It retains the weighting by the probability of destruction, which is lost when we bound the summand
by a multiple of ℓ(Fn,m )/n. Estimating this weighted sum directly is one possible route to a sharper
result.
5.4. The change in the mean when a variable is added. The second deletion identity also
bounds the change in the mean hitting time when one variable is added.
Corollary 5.3. For fixed k ≥ 3 and n > k,
                                        an−1
                                   0≤         − an ≤ Ck .                                            (5.1)
                                      1 − k/n
In particular, |an − an−1 | = Ok (1).
Proof. By (3.4),

                   sn−1 ((1 − k/n)t) − sn (t) = E 1{G is satisfiable} qG (kt/(2n))2 ≥ 0.
Its integral is precisely the difference in (5.1), since 0∞ sn (t) dt = an . Choose a sufficiently
                                                               ∫︁

large constant L = L(k). For n ≥ 2k and 0 ≤ t ≤ Ln, Lemma 2.1 bounds the integrand by
Ck E[1{G is satisfiable} rn−1 (G)−2(k−1)/k ]. Since 2(k − 1)/k > 1, the change of variables and occupation
estimate used in Proposition 3.2 give a bound independent of n. For t > Ln, the difference is at
                                                 k
most sn−1 ((1 − k/n)t) ≤ 2n−1 e−(1−k/n)t/2 , whose integral is exponentially small for sufficiently
large L. Increasing the constant handles k < n < 2k. Finally,

by (2.3) and the bound just proved.                                                                    □
